The card returns B, E." width="100%"} VoteRank (Zhang et al., 2016) picks seed nodes for spreading something (information, a product, an intervention) one at a time by voting. Every node starts with one vote and votes for each of its neighbors; the node with the most votes is elected. The winner then stops voting, and its neighbors' voting ability drops by `1 / average degree`, so the next winner tends to sit in a different part of the network. The result spreads seeds out, avoiding the overlap you get by simply taking the highest-degree nodes. On a directed graph a node collects votes from the nodes it points to, as in NetworkX. Ties go to the lowest node ID. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [count]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : How many spreaders to pick. If `None` (default), keep electing until no node has a positive vote, or every node is chosen. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The elected node IDs, in election order. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `count=` is negative. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Two stars joined by their hubs: VoteRank elects one hub, then the other, rather than two nodes from the same star: ::: {#0265f51c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["h1", "a", "b", "c", "h2", "d", "e", "f"]) .add_edges([("h1", "a"), ("h1", "b"), ("h1", "c"), ("h1", "h2"), ("h2", "d"), ("h2", "e"), ("h2", "f")]) ) [graph.get_label_from_id(n) for n in graph.voterank(count=2)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['h1', 'h2'] ``` ::: :::
